screens.title: Logging for Better Troubleshooting
screens.narratorSegment: In this lesson you will learn why using a dedicated logging system matters more than ad hoc print statements when you build automation that runs without human supervision. Logging gives you structured, persistent records with severity levels, timestamps, and module context so you can diagnose problems from past runs. You will see how Python s standard logging module separates three responsibilities: the logger that creates messages, the handler that sends them to destinations like console or files, and the formatter that shapes what each line looks like. We will walk through configuring loggers to send debug details to a file while limiting console noise to information and warnings. You will also practice including traceback information when exceptions occur, and learn common pitfalls such as over‑logging, relying on default settings that hide info, or using broad exception handlers that swallow useful diagnostics. By the end you will understand how to make a health check script produce an audit trail you can rely on, and you will be able to choose levels and formats that match development and production needs. Think about one script you run unattended; what would you need to see in a log to fix its next failure?

content.html:
Module 4 › Chapter 4.3 › Logging for Better Troubleshooting
Logging for Better Troubleshooting
Make automation observable and debuggable with structured logs that persist.
In this lesson
Why logging replaces print statements for production scripts. How logging levels, handlers, and formatters work. Integrating exception tracebacks and log rotation practices.
Coming up
A live coding demo refactors a health check script to use the logging module, sending debug to file and info to console, plus an exercise to match messages to levels.
Key idea

Use logging to capture severity, context, and persistence. Configure handlers to route verbose output to files and limit console output to meaningful events.

Visual concept
Logger → Handler → Formatter
logger = getLogger(name) handlers = [StreamHandler(), FileHandler('file.log')] formatter = Formatter('%(asctime)s - %(name)s - %(levelname)s - %(message)s')
Explore Key Topics
Levels and filtering
Choose DEBUG through CRITICAL to control verbosity.
Handlers and destinations
Send detailed logs to files and concise ones to console.
Exception tracebacks
Include traceback to diagnose failures that occur in production.

screens.title: Learning Objectives
screens.narratorSegment: By the end of this chapter you will explain why a dedicated logging solution is superior to scattershot print statements, and you will be able to configure Python s logging system for both console and file output. You will distinguish when to use DEBUG, INFO, WARNING, ERROR, and CRITICAL and apply them to real events so your logs are useful instead of noisy. You will format messages to include timestamps, module names, function names, and line numbers so that a future investigator can find the code and context that produced an event. Finally you will integrate logging into automation scripts, making sure exceptions are recorded with their traceback so you can diagnose crashes without an interactive debugger. Each objective is a practical skill: learning not only the names of components but how to configure handlers and formatters, how to choose levels that match development or production, and how to avoid common mistakes like over logging or swallowing exceptions. These skills turn scripts into observable services that you can maintain and troubleshoot reliably.

screens.title: Why logging beats print statements
screens.narratorSegment: Print statements are great for fast, local debugging, but they fall short for any automation you run unattended. A print call always writes to standard output with no severity or context and no easy way to turn it off or redirect it. In contrast, logging gives you severity levels so you can control what gets recorded and what gets ignored. For example, during development you might want a lot of debug details about variable values, while in production you normally want only warnings and errors. With logging you can send debug to a file and keep your console clean with info and above. Logging also attaches context: timestamps, the module or function name, and line numbers that point back to the code path that produced the message. That means when a server runs an automation script daily, you can examine the file to reconstruct what happened hours earlier and where. A common misconception is that logging is only for large applications. In reality, even small automation scripts benefit because logs provide a persistent audit trail. Concrete example: a daily health check that once failed due to a missing config file. A print statement may have scrolled away, but a logged error with traceback and timestamp lets you find the exact failing line and the time it occurred. Takeaway: use logging for durable, contextual diagnostics instead of transient prints.

keyIdea.title: Print vs Logging
keyIdea.text: Print is immediate and transient; logging is structured, filterable, and persistent for production troubleshooting.

content.html:
Module 4 › Chapter 4.3 › Why logging beats print
Definition
Logging records events with severity and context and optionally writes them to different destinations, while print writes plain text to standard output only.
Why it matters
  • Persistence: logs are kept in files for post mortem analysis.
  • Filtering: severity levels let you ignore low importance messages in production.
  • Context: timestamps, module names, and line numbers point to the source.
  • Destination flexibility: same code can send to console, file, or remote endpoints.
Common mistake
Relying on print alone in production leads to missing evidence when failures occur unattended.
Concrete example
# Health check script example output logged to file: 2023-05-01 02:00:01 - health_check - ERROR - check_disk_space - Line 42 - Configuration file 'non_existent_config.txt' not found Traceback (most recent call last):   File "health_check.py", line 42, in check_disk_space     raise FileNotFoundError('...')
This logged error includes timestamp, logger name, severity, function, line, message, and traceback so you can act without attaching a debugger.
Key Takeaway

Logging preserves context and history so you can troubleshoot scripts running unattended.

Misconception

Logging is only for big systems. Small automation benefits equally from persistent logs.

screens.title: Logging levels and when to use them
screens.narratorSegment: Logging levels are how you express the severity or importance of events your code emits. Use DEBUG for highly detailed diagnostic information that helps you understand internal state while developing or reproducing tricky bugs. Use INFO for confirmation that major steps completed successfully, such as a configuration loaded or a scheduled job started. Use WARNING for conditions that are unexpected but do not stop the program, for example threshold values that suggest maintenance is needed. Use ERROR when the program cannot perform a specific function due to a failure, like failing to read a required file. Use CRITICAL when the program may be unable to continue, such as an unrecoverable dependency failure. A common confusion is to log everything at ERROR to ensure visibility; that loses nuance and buries important differences. Instead, choose levels that reflect actionability: INFO to indicate normal progress, WARNING to flag something to check, and ERROR to show failed operations. Concrete example: in a disk check, report used percentage with DEBUG for development, INFO for normal healthy messages, WARNING if usage exceeds a threshold, and ERROR if a check fails due to an exception. Takeaway question: what level would you use for a transient network hiccup that succeeded on retry? Consider WARNING if it recovered but note ERROR if the check failed outright.

keyIdea.title: Levels guide action
keyIdea.text: Choose the level that matches severity and actionability so logs are informative, not noisy.

content.html:
Module 4 › Chapter 4.3 › Logging levels
Level reference
  • DEBUG: Detailed diagnostic information for troubleshooting.
  • INFO: Confirmation that things are working as expected.
  • WARNING: Unexpected events that still allow operation.
  • ERROR: Failures preventing specific operations.
  • CRITICAL: Severe errors indicating the program may stop running.
Example mapping
Disk check successful: INFO
Disk at 85 percent: WARNING
File not found while opening config: ERROR
Unhandled exception preventing run: CRITICAL
Misconception
Logging everything at ERROR or everything at DEBUG is a common mistake. Use levels so the signal to noise ratio remains useful for both developers and operators.
Check your understanding
If a retryable network call failed once but succeeded on retry, what level captures that you should review stability but that the script continued? Hint: this should alert but not treat the run as failed.
Key Takeaway

Use levels to match the severity and likely action; warnings for recoverable issues, errors for failed operations.

screens.title: Logger, Handler, Formatter roles
screens.narratorSegment: The logging system is built from three cooperating parts that let you control emission, destination, and appearance. First, the logger is the object your code calls to create a log record using methods named after levels like debug, info, warning, error, and critical. Loggers are often named by module so you can configure modules independently. Second, handlers decide where records go. Common handlers include a stream handler for the console and a file handler for persistent logs. You can add multiple handlers to a logger to send a single message to several destinations. Third, formatters transform the raw record into a human readable string, allowing you to include a timestamp, the logger name, the level, the function name, line number, and the message. A typical flow is logger creates a record, handlers filter by level and deliver it, and the formatter renders the final text. A misconception is that formatters and handlers are the same; they are separate concerns so you can reuse the same formatter across handlers or apply different formats per destination. Concrete example: send debug rich format to a rotating file handler, while sending a compact timestamped info format to the console. Takeaway: think of loggers as sources, handlers as routers, and formatters as the final presentation.

keyIdea.title: Three responsibilities
keyIdea.text: Logger creates messages, handlers route them, and formatters shape how they look so you can mix and match behavior.

content.html:
Module 4 › Chapter 4.3 › Logger, Handler, Formatter
Logger
Creates log records and exposes the level methods. Named loggers allow per-module configuration and easier filtering.
Handler
Routes records to destinations like console, files, or rotating files. Handlers can set their own level and filters.
Formatter
Defines the textual layout of a record using specifiers for time, name, level, function, line, and message.
Example configuration idea
# Send DEBUG to file with rich detail, INFO to console compact format
This lets you preserve full diagnostics while keeping operational console output readable. If you later add a remote handler you reuse the same formatter or design a new one for machine parsing.
Pro tip

Use named loggers per module so libraries and your application can be tuned independently.

Mistake

Attaching the same handler to multiple loggers without considering levels can duplicate output.

screens.title: Configure basic logging and handlers
screens.narratorSegment: Configuring logging for both file and console typically uses a basic configuration or manual handler setup. You want your file to capture everything useful for post mortem, so set it to capture debug and above. At the same time, set the console stream to a higher level such as info so operators see meaningful messages without debug noise. A practical pattern is to call the logging module s configuration helper with a list of handlers: one file handler and one stream handler. If you use the helper, be mindful that it configures the root logger and may not be suitable for libraries. The example in the chapter shows a configuration where the file handler is left at the root level to capture debug but the stream handler has its level lowered to info after basic configuration. A common trap is assuming stream handlers will respect the basic level automatically; you may need to adjust the handler s level explicitly. Concrete example: configure the root logger to DEBUG and then set the stream handler s level to INFO so debug messages go to the file but not the console. Misconception: calling the basic configuration twice will not automatically merge handlers; configure handlers deliberately and check the resulting handlers list. Takeaway: make the file the comprehensive record and the console the filtered, operator view.

keyIdea.title: Dual-destination setup
keyIdea.text: Configure the file to record debug and above while keeping console output to info and above for operator clarity.

content.html:
Module 4 › Chapter 4.3 › Configure basic logging
Starter snippet
import logging import sys logging.basicConfig( level=logging.DEBUG, format='%(asctime)s - %(name)s - %(levelname)s - %(message)s', handlers=[logging.FileHandler('health_check.log'), logging.StreamHandler(sys.stdout)] ) # Set console to INFO only for operator view for handler in logging.root.handlers: if isinstance(handler, logging.StreamHandler): handler.setLevel(logging.INFO)
This pattern configures the root logger to capture debug but then raises the stream handler threshold to info so the file keeps everything while the console remains readable.
Why adjust handler levels
Handlers can filter records independently so you can route verbose messages to files and concise messages to operators. This avoids changing logging calls across the codebase.
Common mistake
Relying on basic configuration without checking handler levels can leave your console noisier than you expect or your file missing debug messages.
Key Takeaway

Set the root minimum to capture desired levels and tune handlers to direct the right information to each destination.

screens.title: Formatting log messages for context
screens.narratorSegment: A log line is only useful if it points you to the what, when, and where of an event. That is what formatters provide. Use format specifiers to include the human readable creation time, the logger name typically derived from the module, the textual level name, the function and line number, and finally the message. This combination gives you the breadcrumb trail to find the code path and the moment the event occurred. A typical format string includes placeholders for time level and location. In practice you might use a verbose format for file logs and a compact format for console output. A misconception is to put too much sensitive or verbose data into the message; logs can contain configuration values but avoid writing secrets or large binary blobs. Concrete example: include asctime to record the timestamp, name to show the module, levelname for severity, funcName and lineno to find the code, and message for the actual event. In the health check starter script you saw a format that includes all these fields. After formatting, you can parse logs manually or with tools if you preserve key fields consistently. Takeaway: format intentionally so each line answers who what when and where.

keyIdea.title: Format for traceability
keyIdea.text: Design format strings that include timestamp, source module, severity, function, line, and message to speed debugging.

content.html:
Module 4 › Chapter 4.3 › Formatting log messages
Common format specifiers
  • asctime: Human readable creation time of the record.
  • name: Logger name, usually the module name.
  • levelname: The textual logging level.
  • funcName and lineno: Where in the code the call was made.
  • message: The user supplied message.
Verbose file format example
%(asctime)s - %(name)s - %(levelname)s - %(funcName)s - Line %(lineno)d - %(message)s
Console compact format
%(asctime)s - %(levelname)s - %(message)s
Best practice

Balance information and readability. Keep sensitive data out of logs and prefer structured fields for parsing if needed later.

screens.title: Logging exceptions with traceback
screens.narratorSegment: When an exception occurs in a script running unattended, the most important thing is to capture the traceback so you can see the call stack and error message later. The logging methods accept an argument that tells the logger to include exception information in the record. That flag preserves the stack trace which is invaluable for diagnosing crashes. A common mistake is to log only the exception message without the traceback or to swallow the exception in a broad except clause without logging anything. Prefer to catch expected exceptions when you can recover, and log the error with traceback when you cannot. Concrete example from the health check starter: when a file is missing raise a FileNotFoundError and then in the except block call the error method with exc_info set to true so the resulting file log contains the stack trace. If you need to re raise, log first and then re raise or handle accordingly. Another practical tip: avoid logging the same traceback multiple times at different layers unless you add helpful context each time. Takeaway: include the traceback in error and critical logs to save hours of guesswork when investigating failures that occurred out of band.

keyIdea.title: Tracebacks matter
keyIdea.text: Use the exc_info option when logging errors so the log file contains the full traceback for post mortem debugging.

content.html:
Module 4 › Chapter 4.3 › Logging exceptions
Why include tracebacks
Tracebacks show the call stack and exact lines that led to an exception. Without them you often only see the final message and must guess the cause.
Example usage
try:    ...except FileNotFoundError as e:    logger.error('Configuration missing', exc_info=True)
Common mistake
Catching broad exceptions without logging exc_info loses the traceback and makes it hard to find the root cause later.
Practical tip
Log context with the exception for clarity. For example mention which configuration file or host failed so the traceback is easier to interpret.
Key Takeaway

Always include exception tracebacks in error logs to enable reliable post mortem debugging of unattended scripts.

screens.title: Common logging mistakes and how to avoid them
screens.narratorSegment: Understanding common mistakes helps you avoid them before they become costly. One frequent error is not configuring logging at all and relying on defaults that only show warnings and above; this causes missed info during troubleshooting. Another is using print statements instead of logging which lacks levels and routing. A third mistake is over logging at debug level in production which creates noise and large files, or conversely under logging which hides necessary diagnostics. File rotation is often overlooked; logs can grow indefinitely unless you use handlers that rotate files by size or time. Finally, broad exception handlers that do not log exc_info lead to lost tracebacks. For each mistake there is a correction: explicitly configure logging levels and handlers during initialization, replace prints with appropriate logging calls, tune debug usage to development only, add rotating handlers for long running jobs, and always log exceptions with traceback when failure prevents normal operation. Concrete example: attach a rotating file handler that keeps files under control while preserving debug history. Takeaway: be deliberate about configuration so logs remain useful and manageable. Common logging mistakes and how to avoid them means do not rely on defaults, avoid prints in production, balance log volume, rotate files, and always log tracebacks on exceptions.. In practical terms, practical corrections to frequent pitfalls. A concrete example makes the pattern visible, and a brief contrast helps prevent a common misconception. This matters because learners need the underlying reasoning before they can apply the idea confidently or notice where it breaks down. The main takeaway is that the concept should be understood as a meaningful pattern, not just a label on the screen.

Module 4 › Chapter 4.3 › Common mistakes
Mistake vs Fix
No logging configured → Configure root logger and handlers explicitly
Using print → Replace with logger.debug or logger.info depending on severity
Too much debug in production → Use environments to set lower minimum in production
Unrotated large log files → Use RotatingFileHandler or TimedRotatingFileHandler
Catching exceptions without exc_info → Log with exc_info=True
Concrete scenario
A long running cron job filled disk because logs were never rotated. Solution: add a rotating file handler that keeps a fixed number of backups and prevents disk exhaustion while retaining recent history for investigation.

screens.title: Integrating logging into automation scripts
screens.narratorSegment: Integrating logging into an automation script follows a small, repeatable sequence. First, decide the logging policy for that script: which messages must be captured and where they should go. Next, configure the root or named logger early in the script with a file handler that captures debug and a stream handler set to info. Third, replace existing print statements with appropriate logging calls so messages have severity and are discoverable. Fourth, wrap risky operations in try except blocks that log errors with exc_info set so tracebacks are preserved. Fifth, add rotation to long running or frequently executed scripts so logs do not exhaust disk. Finally, when the script matures, consider adding structured logging or JSON formatters for automated log parsing. A concrete example is the health check starter script where the basic configuration is added at the top, debug goes to health_check. log, the console shows only info and above, and exceptions in check functions log with tracebacks. A common misconception is that integration requires massive refactoring; in many cases a few replaces and one configuration block yield most benefits. Takeaway: integrate logging as early as possible and make the file the durable source of truth.

screens.title: Key Concepts — What to Remember
screens.narratorSegment: We close with three compact reminders to guide your practice. First, logging is the durable, configurable replacement for print when scripts must be maintainable and observable. Second, use logging levels intentionally: debug for deep detail, info for normal operation, warning for conditions to watch, error for failed actions, and critical for unrecoverable issues. Third, combine loggers, handlers, and formatters so you can send verbose diagnostics to files and filtered messages to the console, and always include exception tracebacks when handling errors. Together these ideas make automation scripts much easier to troubleshoot without attaching a debugger. A quick check: if you can answer what you would log at INFO versus WARNING for one of your daily tasks, you are ready to apply the configuration patterns from this chapter. Keep logs readable, avoid secrets, and rotate files when a script runs frequently.

fullNarratorScript:
In this lesson you will learn why using a dedicated logging system matters more than ad hoc print statements when you build automation that runs without human supervision. Logging gives you structured, persistent records with severity levels, timestamps, and module context so you can diagnose problems from past runs. You will see how Python s standard logging module separates three responsibilities: the logger that creates messages, the handler that sends them to destinations like console or files, and the formatter that shapes what each line looks like. We will walk through configuring loggers to send debug details to a file while limiting console noise to information and warnings. You will also practice including traceback information when exceptions occur, and learn common pitfalls such as over‑logging, relying on default settings that hide info, or using broad exception handlers that swallow useful diagnostics. By the end you will understand how to make a health check script produce an audit trail you can rely on, and you will be able to choose levels and formats that match development and production needs. Think about one script you run unattended; what would you need to see in a log to fix its next failure?

By the end of this chapter you will explain why a dedicated logging solution is superior to scattershot print statements, and you will be able to configure Python s logging system for both console and file output. You will distinguish when to use DEBUG, INFO, WARNING, ERROR, and CRITICAL and apply them to real events so your logs are useful instead of noisy. You will format messages to include timestamps, module names, function names, and line numbers so that a future investigator can find the code and context that produced an event. Finally you will integrate logging into automation scripts, making sure exceptions are recorded with their traceback so you can diagnose crashes without an interactive debugger. Each objective is a practical skill: learning not only the names of components but how to configure handlers and formatters, how to choose levels that match development or production, and how to avoid common mistakes like over logging or swallowing exceptions. These skills turn scripts into observable services that you can maintain and troubleshoot reliably.

This chapter combines explanation with a hands on activity so you don t just know concepts but can apply them. You will modify a health check script to log to both a file and the console with different minimum levels. The exercise asks you to make the file capture debug and above so every diagnostic event is saved, while the console shows information and above to avoid flooding terminal output. You will practice including timestamps and the module name in the format so each line points to where and when an event happened. Finally, you will update exception handling so errors include their full traceback in the logs. These tasks build muscle memory: run the script, inspect the generated log file, and confirm that warnings and errors appear on the console while debug details are preserved in the file. This workflow is what makes an automated script maintainable and diagnosable in production. After completing the activity you will be able to replicate the configuration in other scripts and adjust levels to match development versus deployment needs.

Print statements are great for fast, local debugging, but they fall short for any automation you run unattended. A print call always writes to standard output with no severity or context and no easy way to turn it off or redirect it. In contrast, logging gives you severity levels so you can control what gets recorded and what gets ignored. For example, during development you might want a lot of debug details about variable values, while in production you normally want only warnings and errors. With logging you can send debug to a file and keep your console clean with info and above. Logging also attaches context: timestamps, the module or function name, and line numbers that point back to the code path that produced the message. That means when a server runs an automation script daily, you can examine the file to reconstruct what happened hours earlier and where. A common misconception is that logging is only for large applications. In reality, even small automation scripts benefit because logs provide a persistent audit trail. Concrete example: a daily health check that once failed due to a missing config file. A print statement may have scrolled away, but a logged error with traceback and timestamp lets you find the exact failing line and the time it occurred. Takeaway: use logging for durable, contextual diagnostics instead of transient prints.

Logging levels are how you express the severity or importance of events your code emits. Use DEBUG for highly detailed diagnostic information that helps you understand internal state while developing or reproducing tricky bugs. Use INFO for confirmation that major steps completed successfully, such as a configuration loaded or a scheduled job started. Use WARNING for conditions that are unexpected but do not stop the program, for example threshold values that suggest maintenance is needed. Use ERROR when the program cannot perform a specific function due to a failure, like failing to read a required file. Use CRITICAL when the program may be unable to continue, such as an unrecoverable dependency failure. A common confusion is to log everything at ERROR to ensure visibility; that loses nuance and buries important differences. Instead, choose levels that reflect actionability: INFO to indicate normal progress, WARNING to flag something to check, and ERROR to show failed operations. Concrete example: in a disk check, report used percentage with DEBUG for development, INFO for normal healthy messages, WARNING if usage exceeds a threshold, and ERROR if a check fails due to an exception. Takeaway question: what level would you use for a transient network hiccup that succeeded on retry? Consider WARNING if it recovered but note ERROR if the check failed outright.

The logging system is built from three cooperating parts that let you control emission, destination, and appearance. First, the logger is the object your code calls to create a log record using methods named after levels like debug, info, warning, error, and critical. Loggers are often named by module so you can configure modules independently. Second, handlers decide where records go. Common handlers include a stream handler for the console and a file handler for persistent logs. You can add multiple handlers to a logger to send a single message to several destinations. Third, formatters transform the raw record into a human readable string, allowing you to include a timestamp, the logger name, the level, the function name, line number, and the message. A typical flow is logger creates a record, handlers filter by level and deliver it, and the formatter renders the final text. A misconception is that formatters and handlers are the same; they are separate concerns so you can reuse the same formatter across handlers or apply different formats per destination. Concrete example: send debug rich format to a rotating file handler, while sending a compact timestamped info format to the console. Takeaway: think of loggers as sources, handlers as routers, and formatters as the final presentation.

Configuring logging for both file and console typically uses a basic configuration or manual handler setup. You want your file to capture everything useful for post mortem, so set it to capture debug and above. At the same time, set the console stream to a higher level such as info so operators see meaningful messages without debug noise. A practical pattern is to call the logging module s configuration helper with a list of handlers: one file handler and one stream handler. If you use the helper, be mindful that it configures the root logger and may not be suitable for libraries. The example in the chapter shows a configuration where the file handler is left at the root level to capture debug but the stream handler has its level lowered to info after basic configuration. A common trap is assuming stream handlers will respect the basic level automatically; you may need to adjust the handler s level explicitly. Concrete example: configure the root logger to DEBUG and then set the stream handler s level to INFO so debug messages go to the file but not the console. Misconception: calling the basic configuration twice will not automatically merge handlers; configure handlers deliberately and check the resulting handlers list. Takeaway: make the file the comprehensive record and the console the filtered, operator view.

A log line is only useful if it points you to the what, when, and where of an event. That is what formatters provide. Use format specifiers to include the human readable creation time, the logger name typically derived from the module, the textual level name, the function and line number, and finally the message. This combination gives you the breadcrumb trail to find the code path and the moment the event occurred. A typical format string includes placeholders for time level and location. In practice you might use a verbose format for file logs and a compact format for console output. A misconception is to put too much sensitive or verbose data into the message; logs can contain configuration values but avoid writing secrets or large binary blobs. Concrete example: include asctime to record the timestamp, name to show the module, levelname for severity, funcName and lineno to find the code, and message for the actual event. In the health check starter script you saw a format that includes all these fields. After formatting, you can parse logs manually or with tools if you preserve key fields consistently. Takeaway: format intentionally so each line answers who what when and where.

When an exception occurs in a script running unattended, the most important thing is to capture the traceback so you can see the call stack and error message later. The logging methods accept an argument that tells the logger to include exception information in the record. That flag preserves the stack trace which is invaluable for diagnosing crashes. A common mistake is to log only the exception message without the traceback or to swallow the exception in a broad except clause without logging anything. Prefer to catch expected exceptions when you can recover, and log the error with traceback when you cannot. Concrete example from the health check starter: when a file is missing raise a FileNotFoundError and then in the except block call the error method with exc_info set to true so the resulting file log contains the stack trace. If you need to re raise, log first and then re raise or handle accordingly. Another practical tip: avoid logging the same traceback multiple times at different layers unless you add helpful context each time. Takeaway: include the traceback in error and critical logs to save hours of guesswork when investigating failures that occurred out of band.

Understanding common mistakes helps you avoid them before they become costly. One frequent error is not configuring logging at all and relying on defaults that only show warnings and above; this causes missed info during troubleshooting. Another is using print statements instead of logging which lacks levels and routing. A third mistake is over logging at debug level in production which creates noise and large files, or conversely under logging which hides necessary diagnostics. File rotation is often overlooked; logs can grow indefinitely unless you use handlers that rotate files by size or time. Finally, broad exception handlers that do not log exc_info lead to lost tracebacks.
